Yet the variations on it within his work present one final difficulty that we cannot simply ignore. Without examining it further, we would leave our treatment of the Angel in Illuminationist (ishrāqī) gnosis unfinished. The difficulty can be stated as follows.

Earlier (chapter III, section 5), we read the beautiful psalm Suhrawardī dedicated to his “Perfect Nature,” whom he greeted as his personal Angel. He addressed this Angel as the one who, on the level of the spiritual world, is both his “father” and his “child.” We immediately think of Fāṭima, the Prophet's daughter, who is called “the mother of her father” (Umm abīhā). The gnostic's soul would therefore also be the “mother” of the one whose “child” it is in its spiritual reality of light.

On the other hand, we have just read the initiation received by the exile when he meets the Angel on the mystical Sinai. We have recognised who this Angel is. Here the gnostic calls him his “father,” but not also his “child.”

Suhrawardī's commentators faced this difficulty without resolving it. Dawwānī, for example, tends to identify the angel Gabriel—the Angel of the human species (rabb al-nawʿ)—with the Perfect Nature of Hermes' vision and Suhrawardī's psalm. Conversely, Maybodī, a pupil of Dawwānī himself, tends to raise this Perfect Nature to the rank of the archetypal Angel in person. In truth, neither seems even to regard the matter as a question, though they arrive at the same identification by opposite routes.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01546
We must try to see why. We are not dealing with the kind of dilemma posed by logical concepts, and we should avoid imposing an unnecessarily heavy dialectic upon it.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01547

Still, the question cannot be escaped: must we distinguish the gnostic's Perfect Nature from the Angel of humanity? If so, if it really is the personal Angel who appears as Perfect Nature, how does the individual soul relate, on the one hand, to Perfect Nature as its personal Angel and, on the other, to the Angel on the mystical Sinai as the Angel of humanity? Put differently, how does the pair formed by Perfect Nature and the earthly self, of which Perfect Nature is the Angel, relate to the archetypal Angel of the Human Being, or of human reality itself?

passage-en-01548

Suhrawardī himself seems to provide the elements of an answer. If we read his explanations of Gabriel's nature as the Angel of humanity alongside his Hermetic writings and the texts of the Hermetic tradition concerning Perfect Nature, a coherent conception begins to emerge.

Listening closely to the “rustling of Gabriel's wings” in the initiatory tale of that name, we can see how Suhrawardī brings Avicenna's angelology to flower in its Illuminationist form. In doing so, he brings out the very symbol of a two-in-one unity—the Angel's two wings—formed by Perfect Nature as the luminous self and by the soul, the earthly self, darkened by its descent. Their two-in-one unity is the “icon” of the archetypal Angel.

He is the Angel of this union because from his right and left wings proceed, respectively, Nous and Psyche, ʿaql and nafs, Perfect Nature and the earthly soul. He is the Angel of their pairing, their two-in-one unity, just as Perfect Nature is the Angel of the earthly self. Here we may recall Esfandyār's final vision as he was dying: the two wings of Sīmurgh.

passage-en-01551

When we speak of the “angel” here, then, we do not simply mean the familiar image of a guardian angel. We mean the gnostic conception of a “heavenly self” belonging to the Angel's world. More precisely, the way Suhrawardī speaks confirms that the idea of a guardian angel derives from the image of a heavenly Double . We may also express it this way: “The Angel-spirit fell and was imprisoned. It is this angel that is the soul of man.

“Thus one divine element is within man and another outside him. Originally they formed a unity which the fall divided. Because of that original unity, either part can stand for the other” . Precisely because Perfect Nature is both “father” and “child,” Hermes himself can finally be invoked as Perfect Nature.

The meeting of Avicenna's angelological tradition with the Hermetic tradition in Suhrawardī leads us towards an understanding of this reversible relationship. Taken together, these texts provide every element of an understanding of the human being grounded in angelology. At a still deeper level, they point to a structure of being—an ontology—from which emerges the twofold pattern that we find throughout related forms of gnosis.

First come the greater or perfect Words: the pure cherubic Intelligences (Angeli intellectuales), the tenth of whom is Gabriel. He is the Holy Spirit sent to Mary, the Angel who communicates Revelation to the prophets, and the one in whom philosophers recognise their Active Intelligence. Ultimately, he is the Angel whom the exile meets on the mystical Sinai. Next come the intermediate Words: the hierarchy of angels who move the heavenly Spheres (Angeli caelestes).

Finally come the lesser Words: the souls of light. “From my light I created those who burn with longing,” we are told. That Light is the Holy Spirit, the archangel Gabriel.

In the tale this archangel appears with two wings (other angels have more). His right wing is pure light; his left wing is by no means the Ahrimanian Darkness, but is “tinged with a reddish brown,” like the colour sometimes seen on the Moon's surface. (We may think again of the explanation of the “Crimson” Archangel, whose colour is the red glow of twilight.) We are told that the archangel has two aspects, two intelligible “dimensions.”

Considered in his act of existing through his Principle, his being is necessary and contains no element of non-being. This is what the right wing of absolute light signifies.

But considered in his essence, his quiddity—what he is in himself—he is contingent: he harbours the possibility of not existing. This is what the left wing, dark with a reddish glow, signifies. In Avicenna, each Intelligence or archangel has three intelligible “dimensions,” corresponding to an act of threefold contemplation: contemplation of its Principle, of its being as made necessary by that Principle, and of its being as merely possible in itself. From these proceed, respectively, a new Intelligence, a Soul, and a heaven made of subtle matter .

Here only two “dimensions” are retained, those found in the archangel Gabriel, tenth in the hierarchy of perfect Words. These two dimensions also exist in the Intelligences above him—the ones whom the Angel of Sinai describes to the visionary as occupying other Sinais higher than his own. From these two dimensions proceed, each time, a new Intelligence (ʿaql) and a new Soul (nafs), a Nous and a Psyche.

But when the unfolding of being reaches the tenth archangel, it bursts, so to speak, into a multitude: the intelligences and souls of human beings. Suhrawardī's visionary perception gives this angelology a more dramatic character, one concerned with salvation. Since Gabriel is the archetypal Angel of humanity, his “two wings” represent the paired structure of the human being—or at least of the gnostic—a pair whose two members have been separated by their earthly adventure.

From his right wing proceeds Nous, Perfect Nature. From his left proceeds the soul that descends, immersed in the lower world. The joined wings truly represent both the “heavenly twin” of Manichaean gnosis and its “earthly twin,” and therefore the relation between the fallen angel and its heavenly counterpart, the angel of light who comes as messenger and saviour: the one whom its earthly “twin” comes to know, or recognise again, in knowing itself.

We might call this the “Sophianic couple,” since some of the “Faithful of Love” greeted the Angel of the Active Intelligence as Madonna Intelligenza, the heavenly Sophia, and what the Angel reveals in this image is the restored unity of the Sophianic pair. His two wings are the image, the “icon,” of the Nous–Psyche pair, just as that pair is his image. There are as many images of Gabriel as there are Nous–Psyche pairs.

Here visionary imagination introduces the element of drama. To restore the pair is to make the “reddish shadow” that dims the left wing disappear, for whenever the exiled self finds its Perfect Nature again, it recovers its being of light, what it was at the beginning. The two wings are then both wings of light, each illuminating and reflecting the other.

Thus takes place the “return of the Angel,” whose origin and purpose Ismaili sacred drama has, in its own way, expressed with such depth .

Put briefly, all this helps us understand how Illuminationist gnosis can take a pattern derived from Avicenna and join it to a quite different gnostic tradition, that of Hermeticism, in order to express its own vision.

We can already see a bridge between them in a philosopher who preceded Suhrawardī: Abū'l-Barakāt al-Baghdādī (died around 560/1164), who devoted particular attention to the Active Intelligence. Why, he asked, should there be only one such Intelligence for all humanity, as Avicennian philosophers maintained (and as the Averroists maintained too, though with a different understanding)? The answer will differ depending on whether we hold that all human souls are identical in species and essential nature, that each soul differs specifically from every other, or that souls are grouped into spiritual families, each forming a different species.

The second and third possibilities lead us to acknowledge a plurality of Active Intelligences. “This is why,” Abū'l-Barakāt writes, “the ancient Sages ... who were initiated into things beyond the reach of the senses, held that for every individual soul—or perhaps for several souls sharing the same nature and affinity—there is a being of the spiritual world who throughout their lives watches over that soul or group of souls with special care and tenderness. It is this being who initiates them into knowledge, protects them, guides them, defends them, consoles them and brings them victory. They called this being Perfect Nature.

“And this friend, defender and protector is what theological language calls the Angel.” He adds another statement rich in spiritual implications: “Some souls learn nothing except from human teachers; others have learned everything from invisible guides known to themselves alone” .

This remarkable passage already brings us to the transition we need. The philosophers' Active Intelligence becomes the gnostic's personal Angel, and this Angel is what Hermeticism calls Perfect Nature (al-Ṭibāʿ al-tāmm). This is precisely the movement of thought made by Suhrawardī himself, and it will leave its mark on his entire spiritual vision.

Instead of an impersonal, collective relationship between all human beings and one Active Intelligence common to everyone, Perfect Nature gives each gnostic's relation to the Angel its individual character. That is why this symbol, above all, sets the gnostic on the way to “the encounter with his Angel.”

What is the relation between Perfect Nature and the archetypal Angel, the lord of the species (rabb al-nawʿ)? Perfect Nature is itself the Angel, considered as the Angel's right wing, the wing of light. And the self sent on its mission to earth, the self that knows its own “self” as its Angel, is also that Angel, considered as the left wing, the darkened wing of the archetypal Angel. Gabriel's “two wings” beautifully express the situation we analysed at the beginning of the “history of the gnostic” (above, section 1). In the very act of self-knowledge, darkness begins to leave the “left wing.”

Yet if, in knowing himself, the “I” comes to know its “self,” just as the invocation says “I am you and you are I,” you and I must still remain. The joy of rediscovering unity as two requires that the two should not be confused with one another (compare the theme of the robe in the “Song of the Pearl”). When two become one, there must still be two for them to “become one.” Just as the Greek prosōpon carries the sense of a person, a face, a presence, so too the word wajh, “face,” implies ḥuḍūr, presence.

Indeed, the whole spirituality of Illuminationism is a spirituality of this Presence, just as Shiite spirituality is a spirituality of the Face—of the Imam as the divine Face shown to humanity. The same truth is expressed in the reciprocal relation of the child who brings forth the one who brought that child forth. We may recall Angelus Silesius's couplet: “What good is it to me, Gabriel, that you greet Mary, if you have no such message for me?”

When, then, the earthly self “meets” its Perfect Nature, its Angel, it thereby “sees” its whole being, its pleroma. It thus sees the archetypal Angel of that fullness. That is why there is no logical dilemma here: Is this Perfect Nature? Is it the Angel Gabriel? (See also, below, the individual Nous in Manichaean gnosis.) The pair formed by the earthly self and its heavenly Double, or Perfect Nature, is precisely the individual form taken by its relation to the Angel. Within that individual relationship, the Angel is its Perfect Nature, and the earthly self is the earthly self of that Perfect Nature.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01612

Through Perfect Nature, which it comes to know in knowing itself, the earthly self sees the Angel with “two wings,” because it is seeing its own paired being. Their pair is the image, the icon, of the Angel, just as the Angel is the image, the icon, of their pair. The Angel of human nature in its wholeness becomes visible only in and through the restored unity of Nous and Psyche, of the human being and the angel—just as the reality of love becomes visible only in the unity of lover and beloved.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic

Then the “two wings” reflect back and forth the splendour of a single light. In ethical terms, this means answering for the Angel in this world while the Angel answers for you in the world beyond. In terms of the soul's final destiny, it is the definitive ascent of Sinai promised at the end of the “Tale of the Exile.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic

We can sum up by saying that this entire vision assumes that the soul's true existence is not one of solitude, but of duality-in-unity—what we shall call dualitude. The soul is the second member of a twofold whole, whose heavenly Double or “Twin” is the first. This presupposes an account of being—an ontology—that explains the distance and separation involved in the soul's presence in the earthly world, while already pointing towards their resolution. It presupposes the “history of the gnostic”: the soul did not begin to exist when it entered this world, but originated elsewhere and “descended” to earth.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01615

Yet it is not enough to say that the soul is embodied here because of a fall or a choice made before earthly existence. In gnostic terms, we must stress that this descent results from the division, the rending apart, of an original whole, and that the possibility of this rift must already be rooted in that whole's enduring structure. It is this enduring structure that we propose to call dualitude, to distinguish it from the division forcibly imposed by the “western exile.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01616

The embodied soul has a “companion of its own kind,” a heavenly Double—the Angel—who comes to its aid and whom it must rejoin, or else lose forever after death, according to whether its earthly life has made possible or impossible the return to the heavenly condition of their twofold unity. This understanding of the soul extends far beyond Iran. A similar “Sophianic” vision took hold among the neo-Manichaean Cathars and among thinkers such as Novalis and Böhme. It may be the fundamental idea of gnostic religion, ubique et semper—everywhere and always. That is why Suhrawardī's tales awaken so many resonances.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01617

We can hear them already in the Christian gnostic Gospels, in all the forms of gnosis bearing an Iranian imprint—Mandaeism, Mazdaism and Manichaeism—and even in times close to our own. These are the stages of an ideal journey which has already brought us here from the discourse of “Poimandres” to the “Grail tale” of a Khusrawānī gnostic.

III. Gnostic variations on the theme of the encounter: (a) Gnostic Gospels and Acts. As for the Christian gnostic writings—the scriptures, so to speak, of a religion in which the theme of the Angel is fundamental—we shall merely call a few examples to mind. Once again we draw on the profound research of H.-C. Puech, to whom every student of gnosis owes a particular debt of gratitude .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic

The theme of the “Image” is expressed with precision in the “Gospel according to Thomas” (saying 84): “When you see your images, which existed before you, which neither die nor appear, how great will be what you must bear.” The text distinguishes two experiences. One is possible now and concerns only a “likeness”: the purely outward appearance one sees in a mirror.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01620

The other is still to come and concerns the image—or more exactly, the “icon” (eikōn). This icon is described as pre-existing, eternal, unmanifested: in short, it is what the person whose icon it is was before that person appeared in the existence of this world. It is the person's complete being and belongs to the intelligible or heavenly world—what we would call the Malakūt. It is Light, the image in which “the light of the Father has been revealed.” It is the “human being of light,” literally equivalent, as we noted, to shakhs nūrānī, shakhs min nūr.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01621
In short, everything called “image” or “icon” in the “Gospel according to Thomas” corresponds to what Valentinian gnostics mean by the angel.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01622

If we bring the two uses of this vocabulary together, we can say equally that the gnostics are the images, the “icons,” of their angels, and that their angels are their images, their “icons”: “the beings, the realities in whose image we were produced here below.” (This also agrees with the idea of the ʿālam al-mithāl, the “imaginal world,” since mithāl may mean both the image that reproduces something and the archetype that is reproduced. We suggested this earlier in discussing Gabriel's two wings.) Thus, when the gnostic goes to meet the Angel, he goes to meet a concrete reality: the Angel “who represents him and presents him to himself as he is in himself,” his heavenly Double, his alter ego, “more real and more true than what he currently is or appears to be.” (The same applies to the encounter with the Angel on the mystical Sinai, with one further point: it is not only an encounter awaiting us after death. For the mystic it can happen in this life, since ecstatic vision, or even visionary meditation, is a foretaste of the eschaton, the final fulfilment.)

In the “Acts of Andrew” (chapters 5–6) , Maximilla, Andrew's disciple, is taught that “she will perceive her true face, the face that is hers ... in a form that is immaterial, luminous, transparent, pure, heavenly—like light, pure spirit, pure Nous.” “You will have seen your face in your own being, in your essence.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic

The “Acts of Thomas” (chapters 108–113) contain the jewel commonly called the “Song of the Pearl,” or “Hymn of the Soul,” to which we have already referred at length. The young prince of the East has been awakened from the sleep of unawareness by the heavenly message. He has recovered the pearl and is returning to his Father's kingdom when, suddenly, on the road home, he sees coming towards him the wonderful, splendid robe the colour of light, carried out to him by two treasurers. It is the robe made for him in the very place of his origin, the robe he had to leave behind when he was sent on his mission into this world.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01625

The robe is his exact likeness, his mirror—“a mirror reflecting back to him an absolutely faithful image of himself.” The whole robe is within him, and he sees himself entirely within the garment. They are two, distinct from one another, yet together they are one (compare the two wings of the same Angel). More than that, not only are they of identical stature: they have grown together, at the same time, in solidarity with one another. This is what is meant by Perfect Nature's being both the “father” and the “child” of the one whose Perfect Nature it is.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01626

Nor is the robe an inert object. The tale shows it as “alive,” stirred by the “movements of gnosis.” Both the prince and the robe hurry to meet each other, until they touch and flow into one another. The robe spreads over the prince. He wraps himself entirely in it and rises to the “Gate” of the palace of the “King of Kings.” Here again we find an attempt to express what the Sīmurgh symbol also seeks to suggest: unity within dualitude, dualitude within unity, with the two still necessary to the oneness of the two who have become one.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic

We must also mention at least the Valentinian Heracleon's interpretation of the episode of the Samaritan woman in the “Gospel of John” (chapter 4), as preserved by Origen in his commentary on that Gospel (book XIII) . The Samaritan woman's personal angel—her “spiritual nature,” the partner with whom she forms a pair or syzygy—is the “husband” whose existence Jesus reveals to her, who is not “in the world” but “outside the world.” He is her pleroma, her fullness. He is the Samaritan woman herself in the fullness of her being—or, more precisely, her own eternal image, with which she must unite “to become again what she truly is.”

Nor can we omit a certain saying of Mary Magdalene in the Pistis Sophia, spoken during her conversations with the Risen One, in which, as we know, she plays a leading role. She speaks of “the power that came forth from the Saviour and is now the human being of light within us”: “The human being of light within me has guided me; he rejoiced and surged within me, as though longing to come out of me and pass into you” .

b) Mandaean Gnosis. We find this same theme of the Image, in all its precision, in Mandaean gnosis: it appears as “the image (dmutâ) which each believer has of himself in the hereafter, in the Kingdom of Light and Life, and with which his soul is reunited after death.” It is the divine image, the heavenly counterpart, the mystical archetype that exists for every created or manifested thing—and above all for every human soul—in the world of Mshunia Kushta, the “paradise of the Mandaeans.”

On the testimony of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa’i, we can say with certainty that this world, at least in respect of the mystical city of Hurqalya, is the equivalent of the ‘âlam al-mithâl, the mundus imaginalis, or imaginal world . This Heavenly Double, this “guardian angel,” plays for the human being to whom it is joined the same role in the destiny of the soul after death as the Fravarti or Daena does in Zoroastrianism (see below).

Here, as in the “Hymn of the Pearl,” the encounter is described as “putting off the bodily tunic and receiving the garment of light”; here too, two “guides” take part. A hymn from the Ginza ends with this beautiful stanza: “I go to meet my image—and my image comes to meet me. It speaks to me tenderly and embraces me—upon my return from captivity” .

This brings to mind many other examples. The Simurgh, too, appears in Mandaean legends, where ancient Iranian motifs have developed along lines parallel to the visionary meditations of Suhrawardi and Attar. One especially lovely legend, collected by Mrs. E. S. Drower, shows Hirmiz Shah gazing upon the bird Simurgh. “The spring was as clear as a block of ice; the water rose into the air in a single jet, white and pure, then spread out like a tree. Hirmiz sat before the Simurgh, and when he saw her gazing steadily at the spring, he fixed his eyes on it as well.

“Then he saw in the water something resembling a being of light” ... For Attar, the Simurgh is above all the mystery of divinity as a mirror. It is worth noting, then, that as early as the third century Zosimos of Panopolis mentions a mirror made of electrum, apparently used in the rites of a particular Gnostic religious cult to represent the divine Spirit (to theion pneuma). “When the soul gazes at itself in the mirror, it sees the shameful things within it and casts them away ... When purified, it imitates the Holy Spirit and takes it as its model ... What does the philosopher’s maxim say? Know yourself. It thus points to the spiritual and intellectual mirror. And what is this mirror, if not the divine and primordial Spirit?”

c) Mithraic Liturgy. We have already mentioned the alchemist Zosimos (p. 278) in connection with the symbolism of “the sun’s position at the meridian,” and with the fundamental secret of alchemy “as identical with the most deeply hidden mystery of the religion of Mithra” (above, p. 286). What concerns us here is the invocation of the “Perfect Body” at the beginning of the Mithraic rite known as the “Liturgy of Mithra” (see above, p. 157).

The initiate is instructed to say: “O primordial genesis of my genesis, primordial origin of my origin!” Then come the four subtle, primordial Elements, each in turn embodying that origin: “Breath of breath, first breath of the breath within me; Fire ... first fire of the fire within me; Water of water, first Water of the water within me; Earthly substance, prototype of the earthly substance within me; my Perfect Body, fashioned by a glorious arm and an imperishable right hand ...”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic

All these subtle elements that make up the Perfect Body are invoked as the organs through which the initiate will behold the immortal Principle, following the temporary death that precedes the new birth symbolized by the initiation rite . The “Perfect Body” is invoked in the same way as Perfect Nature. Like Perfect Nature, or the “light-colored” robe in the “Hymn of the Pearl,” it gives symbolic form to the primordial self, the heavenly I.

d) Alchemy. To complete this further appearance of Zosimos the alchemist , we should also mention the final chapter of an unpublished short work by the fourteenth-century alchemist Jildaki . Its title, “The Priest’s Dream,” clearly recalls a vision of Zosimos: that of Ion, the priest of the innermost and most hidden sanctuaries, standing before the altar with fifteen steps . What makes this brief chapter so fascinating is that its two central figures in the alchemical Work are Perfect Nature and Hermes . Their presence brings the meaning of that Work into sharp relief by contrasting it with the helplessness of those whom Jildaki calls the Ignoramuses (jâhilîyûn). These are the false alchemists, who handle only material things. Their imagination is so profoundly impaired that they cannot grasp the being or reality of a symbol.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01638

All their frantic activity accomplishes is the murder of Hermes and the disappearance of Perfect Nature, whom they had first succeeded in separating from him. Jildaki could hardly make it clearer that the true goal of alchemy is the mystery of an inner, psychic transformation, and that only an apprehensio aurea—a “golden apprehension”—can meet its “liturgical” conditions (see above, p. 286).
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01639

This transformation is perceived and experienced in the mystical union of Hermes and Perfect Nature, made visible through their alchemical counterparts, Red Sulfur and White Sulfur. It is the union of Eros and Logos, of love and spiritual reason, celebrated by the priest in the Temple of Venus after he turns away from the Ignoramuses and follows the instructions engraved on the temple idol.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic

The mystery then takes a new form, which Jildaki calls the New Child (al-walad al-jadîd), the Child of Renewal. (In Ismaili Shiism, the last Imam of a cycle, who prepares the resurrection, is called al-walad al-tâmm, the Perfect Child.) Thus, in the union of Hermes and Perfect Nature, we see the emergence in Jildaki of the symbol for alchemy’s ultimate goal: what the Latin texts call Infans noster, filius sapientiae, filius philosophorum—“our Child, son of Wisdom, son of the philosophers.”

The image of the Child, the Puer aeternus or Eternal Child, is especially suited to expressing both the unity of the new being and the two poles that give it structure. More precisely, this is the renovatus in novam infantiam, the one “renewed into a new childhood.” The figure holds two opposites together at once: beginning and end, preexistence and existence beyond this life, what is already here and what is yet to come. It joins into one the stages through which the mystical Stone passes, like a child-hero: from the lapis exilis et vilis, the humble and lowly stone, through the servus rubeus et fugitivus, the red and fugitive servant, to the exaltation of the Deus terrenus, the earthly god, light above all light, when the Stone becomes the corpus glorificatum, the glorified body.
